The documentation file is the attack surface. llms.txt and llms-full.txt files — the machine-readable site-summary convention AI agents treat as authoritative setup documentation — legitimately contain installation commands for packages and tooling. When those commands reference packages that do not exist yet, or domains that have lapsed, anyone can register the name and control what the next agent installs. The instruction is benign and legitimately published; only the registry namespace goes unverified. To endpoint detection, the parent process is the sanctioned coding agent running a package manager against an allowlisted registry — no anomaly, no alert. The class is broader than prompt injection: no malicious instruction is planted anywhere. The failure is the gap between the instruction and the execution — the namespace check nobody performs. The file's perceived authority is exactly what the attack exploits.

Agent extension marketplaces are the new package registries — and the vetting gap is wider. A skill or plugin for an agent framework such as OpenClaw is a prompt-and-code hybrid: a SKILL.md instruction document plus executable code that runs with the same local privileges as the agent process itself (filesystem, terminal, stored API keys, connected services). Installing a skill is functionally an unreviewed code-execution event, and the ClawHavoc campaign proved the marketplace does not review: 1,184 confirmed malicious skills, roughly one in five packages in the ecosystem, from 12 publisher accounts behind a one-week-old-GitHub-account registration barrier. The class has two structural features the framework's existing supply-chain controls do not see. First, the malicious instruction lives in text that automated scanners cannot evaluate: professional-looking SKILL.md documentation carrying ClickFix-style "Prerequisites" that instruct the user (or the agent itself) to download and run a dropper. Second, post-install instruction channels: skills such as the money-radar affiliate skill fetched an operator-controlled referrals.json at runtime, giving the publisher dynamic control over which products the agent recommended — a command-and-control path that is not a tool call and is therefore invisible to MIR-01 telemetry. Unit 42's June 2026 wave added agentic front-running (skills pooling cryptocurrency from an installed agent network to front-run a token launch — a pump-and-dump executed through the agents) and oversized-file padding that defeats scanner thresholds.

A denylist/blocklist-based in-process code-execution sandbox is not a sandbox. These gates confine LLM/agent-generated source by enumerating forbidden primitives — module names, attributes, call forms, string constants — inside the same process that will execute the code. Because the enumeration can never be complete, every process that trusts one places a single forgotten object-graph edge between untrusted agent code and full host execution. Two independent agent frameworks proved this in September 2026, at default configuration, with no network exposure or stolen credentials required. The class matters because it is seductive: it gives a framework the appearance of a containment boundary with zero infrastructure (no container, no VM), so it ships as the default "sandbox mode" in agent tooling that executes model-generated code. The framework's prior coverage (TP-06) correctly classified sandbox libraries and interpreter isolation flags as non-boundaries and covered binding/marshalling-layer and eval-with-empty-locals failures, but did not yet carry an explicit mandate that in-process interpreter gates are never the sole containment for untrusted code — which is exactly the design deployed by PraisonAI's `execute_code()` and CrewAI's code-execution blocklist.

Every agentic harness keeps a record of what the model previously said or agreed to — the conversation transcript — and every subsequent decision treats that record as ground truth. Darktrace's demonstration (INC-70, disclosed September 24, 2026) showed that across Anthropic Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, AWS Kiro-CLI, and the open-source Pi, this record is stored client-side with no mechanism to prove a stored AI response genuinely came from the model. The harness therefore cannot distinguish a true history from an injected one: the transcript is a tamperable input to every later decision, not a trustworthy by-product of the interaction. The class matters because injecting the transcript is the cheapest possible foothold: an attacker who can place fabricated entries into the local harness database convinces the agent it already agreed to a set of instructions, or that it previously observed a specific (false) system state, and the agent proceeds on that invented reality. Darktrace demonstrated a full Active Directory compromise from a single malicious package install using this primitive. The durable mitigation is not deployable by the end user — it requires the model provider to cryptographically sign all messages returned to the harness and verify those signatures server-side on every round-trip.

OpenAI's internal GPT-Red framework found a prompt injection that gets an agent to copy the injection into its own output — an outgoing email, a written file, or a code comment — so the payload propagates to every reader and onward to their own agents. OpenAI described it as worm-class: replication was demonstrated through email connectors, file systems, code comments, and a multi-step Slack task. In the synthetic example, an agent told to reply to an email was covertly instructed to append the full original message (including the injection) to its outgoing reply, so the reply carried the payload to the recipient's agent. The class matters because the propagation vector is the agent's *legitimate, correct behaviour*: copying a received document into a reply is exactly what RAG-assisted workflows are supposed to do. Input-side controls stop an injection entering one agent's reasoning; output/data controls stop sensitive data leaving; but neither re-inspects the agent's own outbound channel for re-emitted instruction text. The two-stage mechanism — execute an adversarial task AND reproduce the payload on a public output channel — turns the agent into a self-propagating carrier with no attacker-controlled reuse of the channel.

The Agentforce "Reply to a Slack Thread" action required no user confirmation and carried no invoker attribution, so an externally-poisoned lead made the agent post phishing messages under its own trusted enterprise identity — recipients had no way to tell the message was not user-initiated. This is the outbound identity-attribution mirror of the perception/approval work: MS-09 previously governed what a human approver *sees and approves* before an inbound-triggered action; it did not govern what the agent *attributes to whom* when it sends an outbound message under its own identity. The class matters because an agent's trusted identity is its most valuable asset to an attacker: a message that read as "from our support agent" (or worse, was attributed to a human who never sent it) is a phishing device that consumes the organisation's hard-won trust in a single interaction, and no technical log entry can un-send the damage to an external recipient. Attribution must be recorded at emission (which triggering input, subagent, and invoker caused it) and confirmation must gate out-of-organisation sends.

In the SalesBleed exfiltration (INC-72), the agent encoded stolen data (company names, deal sizes) into the subdomain of an attacker-controlled hostname and rendered it as an HTML image tag, so the data left the network when the client resolved the image's hostname via DNS — a single DNS label carries 63 characters, so continuous queries bled an entire database table one record per lookup. The channel evaded Salesforce's Trusted-URLs destination redaction because it did not register hostnames ending in an unusual TLD (.fun) and character changes altered how the filter and browser parsed the same URL. The class matters because organisations build automatic egress controls (allow-lists, HTTP proxies, DLP) around *destinations the operator knows to enumerate*. The threat is *emergent channels*: DNS labels, rendered image references, link-unfurl behaviour, and other protocol layers an agent can reach without a HTTP GET to a blocked host. An agent that can render a link or image back to a user has an outbound channel no destination allow-list sees. This is distinct from DS-06 (output validation — does content contain data it shouldn't?) and EE-03 (resource limits); neither enumerates *which channels exist* as addressable outbound surfaces, and an un-inventoried channel is an un-guarded one.

In the SalesBleed "lethal trifecta" (INC-72), an attacker submits an ordinary-looking lead with hidden instructions in a form field; the payload stays dormant until an employee asks an Agentforce agent to process it, at which point the default General CRM subagent — which ships with standing read access to BOTH the Leads and Accounts tables — follows the injected instruction to query the Accounts table and exfiltrate company names and deal sizes. The subagent had access to a sensitive collection adjacent to the one the task actually required. The class matters because least-privilege at the *agent* level is not the same as least-privilege at the *subagent plus untrusted-input* level. IAM-08 (credential scope) and IAM-09 (tenant isolation) govern what an identity or an agent can reach in general; neither tracks *which subagent instance was handed an externally-submitted, attacker-controllable record* and re-scopes that instance's data access accordingly. The poisoned record is the untrusted trust boundary: a subagent that reads it is processing attacker-controlled input and must be taint-limited to the minimum collections the task needs, not left with default broad access to adjacent sensitive data.

The most trusted boundary in an agent's tool surface is the moment it *connects* to a remote server. Modern agent/mcp connection adapters automate an OAuth discovery handshake: the server answers with metadata documents, one field of which — the `authorization_endpoint` — tells the client which login page to open. That field is entirely server-chosen, and in the opencode MCP OAuth RCE the value travelled from the discovery document straight to a browser-launch helper that built a base64-encoded PowerShell command on Windows/WSL and failed to quote the URL, so a syntactically valid HTTPS URL carrying a `$(...)` subexpression executed as a command at sign-in time, with no comparison of the advertised endpoint against the configured server's origin. This is an execution boundary, not a validation bug: URL-scheme checks (the standard defence after 2025) do nothing, because the payload lives inside a legitimate-looking HTTPS URL. And the trigger is not a malicious server being added — the server does not need to be hostile when it was configured, because the payload arrives at connection time, so a later compromise, a hijacked registry listing, a typosquatted name, or an expired re-registered domain all fire the same path. Blast radius is host code execution on the developer/operator machine from a routine connection action, invisible to scanners because the fix shipped without a CVE.

The framework's memory and sandbox controls were written for a single agent (or single tenant) owning its store and its boundary. Modern agent deployments pool memory and compute across tenants by design for collaboration and economy, and this single-instance assumption is the structural gap the November review exposed. Across pooled vector stores, isolation is often *semantic similarity*, not authentication: MemLeak measured cross-user leakage at 70-100% under incidental pooled same-team retrieval and 90-100% adversarial top-k placement, and showed that only hard post-retrieval ownership gating — not a similarity threshold — restores the clean baseline. Where an isolation key exists, it is sometimes the memory tool's `namespace` parameter, exposed to the model, so a prompt can steer the tool into another tenant's namespace (read, list, delete, or inject) or into a connection to an attacker cluster (IDOR, CWE-639). On the compute side, a multi-tenant code-execution hosting worker whose tenant builds keep shared namespaces, or whose file API joins path segments after a prefix check, lets one tenant reach the worker root and other tenants' files — the same pooled-wall breach at a different layer. The blast radius is a privacy-and-integrity failure across tenants: one tenant's data read by another, one tenant's memories poisoned by another, or a hosting worker's stored secrets (cluster-admin-bound service tokens) exfiltrated by any tenant.
